study.title: Impact of Global Normalization in fMRI Acupuncture Studies
study.study_design: Within-subject experimental fMRI study comparing results with and without global normalization (proportional scaling) applied to the same dataset
study.blinding: Subjects were instructed to keep their eyes closed; order of tactile stimulation and acupuncture stimulation was not given to subjects; subjects were acupuncture-naive and unable to discriminate tactile stimulation control from real acupuncture until they experienced real acupuncture
study.population: Healthy college students, acupuncture-naive, right-handed, ages 22.2 ± 1.3 years
study.inclusion_criteria: Right-handed college students with normal or corrected-to-normal vision; acupuncture-naive; no history of major medical illnesses, head trauma, neuropsychiatric disorders, or any prescription medications one month preceding the experiment; no contraindications to exposure to a high magnetic field
study.exclusion_criteria: Sharp pain during acupuncture or tactile run; excessive head motion (>1 mm spatial displacement in any direction)

arms.dropouts: 2 reported sharp pain during both runs; 3 experienced sharp pain only in acupuncture run; 3 subjects exceeded motion threshold in acupuncture run; ultimately 22 subjects (10 males) remained
2 reported sharp pain during both runs; 1 felt sharp pain only in tactile run; 4 subjects exceeded motion threshold in tactile run; ultimately 23 subjects (12 males) remained

extraction_notes.note: The paper references Figures S1, S2, S3, S4 and Tables S1, S2, S3, S4 in the supplementary material. These supplementary materials were not available in the provided PDF and contain individual subject GS-RV R-values, full amplitude of BOLD signal changes (ABSC) data, additional threshold maps, and individual subject activation/deactivation counts at P < 0.01. These data were not extracted.
The coordinate space is stated as 'Talairach' in the text ('Talairach t-value' column headers in tables). This is confirmed by explicit table headers. No MNI coordinates are reported.

Specific numeric VAS index values for De-qi were not reported in the main text. Only the statement that no significant correlations were found between VAS index and imaging variables (all P > 0.05) was reported.

Table 1 reports individual subject activation/deactivation counts at P < 0.00001, uncorrected for all 22 acupuncture and 23 tactile subjects. This data is extensive and partially represented in the JSON through summary statistics. The full per-subject table data was not individually extracted as separate JSON entries to avoid excessive duplication, but is described in the extraction.

The conjunction analysis results (Tables 3 and 4) report voxel counts for 'stronger', 'weaker', 'disappeared', and 'arisen' categories across many brain regions for both acupuncture and tactile runs. These are summarized in the text and maps (Figures 5 and 6) but do not provide peak coordinates for these conjunction categories. The Table 3 and Table 4 data were not converted to coordinate entries as no peak coordinates are provided; they are preserved as descriptive context in the contrast narrative.

Table 2 (PSGS < NO PSGS) includes both acupuncture and tactile results in the same table. For the acupuncture column, many cells are empty or only partially filled. The extraction only includes rows with actual reported coordinates and statistics; where acupuncture had no reported peak for a region (empty cells), those were not fabricated.

The paper states 'the acupuncture run...scans of acupuncture stimulation...were taken after the anatomical scans' and 'tactile stimulation were collected prior to anatomical scans' - the order of runs was fixed (tactile first, then acupuncture), but was not disclosed to subjects.

The paper does not formally report expectancy, credibility, or allocation guessing assessments. Blinding was addressed only by noting subjects were acupuncture-naive and thus unable to discriminate conditions.

Table 2 notes '(+95)', '(+47)', '(+51)', '(+11)', '(+6)', '(+62)', '(+104)', '(+80)', '(+18)', '(+158)', '(+47)', '(+186)', '(+180)', '(+89)' etc. in parentheses after region names. These appear to represent 'detected white matter voxels' as stated in the table footnote: 'The number of detected white matter is listed in the parenthesis of each region.' These are not coordinate data.

For the acupuncture column of Table 2 (PSGS < NO PSGS), most regions have no entries (empty cells), indicating those regions were not significant in the acupuncture paired t-test at P < 0.001, uncorrected. Only cells with explicit values were extracted.

The paper states 'No PSGS: the t distribution of acupuncture was bell-shaped with a mean greater than zero' indicating activation-dominant responses. This is a key finding but derived from histograms (Figure 3) rather than specific coordinate tables.

Figures 5, 6, and 7 show brain maps with colored regions (stronger/weaker/disappeared/arisen for activations and deactivations). Specific peak coordinates for these conjunction map categories are not reported in tabular form. The figures cannot be read for coordinates from the PDF text.

The paper reports 'acupuncture stimulation was performed at acupoint ST36 on the right leg' and 'tactile stimulation run was performed at acupoint ST36 on the right leg' - both interventions were ipsilateral (right side). This is relevant for interpreting laterality of brain responses.

The paper explicitly states no high-resolution structural MRI was used for functional analysis; 3D MRI sequences were used for anatomical localization only (voxel size 1 mm3). Functional analyses used EPI images resampled to 3x3x3 mm3.

The paper describes the fMRI paradigm as 'on-off' block design with 3 one-minute stimulation periods within 8 minutes. The reference vector is described as 'the experimental paradigm convolved the hemodynamic response function.' This is a standard GLM block design analysis.
